chunks.text: 4 Numerical Results We evaluated the proposed method from data obtained from a custom ISM system equipped with a 5 × 5 5\times 5 SPAD detector array [ 8 ] . We chose for ( DIP-ISM ) to reconstruct the specimen 𝐱 \mathbf{x} using 𝐠 𝐱 \mathbf{g}_{\mathbf{x}} as a convolutional skip network, following the architecture used in SelfDeblur [ 9 ] , while 𝐠 𝐡 \mathbf{g}_{\mathbf{h}} was taken as a two-layer fully connected network with ReLU6 activation, followed by Softplus and L 1 L_{1} normalization. We optimize jointly the three networks by doing 10 3 10^{3} Adam steps, with image and kernel learning rates of 10 − 2 10^{-2} and 10 − 4 10^{-4} respectively, to minimize ℒ \mathcal{L} . For comparison, we used MID [ 13 ] , which reconstructs the image through a multi-image Richardson–Lucy scheme using the 25 detector-dependent PSFs 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} constructed from excitation and emission PSFs calculated using vectorial diffraction theory. We also evaluated a non-blind DIP approach using the same fixed theoretical PSFs, providing a baseline for assessing the benefit of joint image and PSF estimation. 4.1 Qualitative comparison Figure 1 compares the conventional confocal image (obtained by summing all the scanned images), the theoretical and estimated effective PSFs, and the three image reconstructions. All three reconstruction methods resolve the main network of tubulin filaments. Compared with MID and DIP with fixed theoretical PSFs, blind DIP produces visually more pronounced fine filament structures, which may reflect its ability to account for optical aberrations affecting the acquisition. The recovered effective PSFs differ from the theoretical ones in their apparent extent and spatial distribution ( fig. 1 ). A main advantage of our ( DIP-ISM ) method is that we recover the underlying excitation and emission PSFs which allow a much finer analysis of the optical system. For example, in fig.

2 the estimated excitation PSF has a diagonally elongated central lobe, consistent with astigmatism, a typical optical aberration that could then be corrected. In these estimated PSFs, the peripheral intensity on the border is not optically plausible and probably reflects an artifact of the blind estimation. However, these peripheral artefacts are largely suppressed in 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} by the pointwise multiplication of the spatially localised excitation and detection PSFs. Figure 2: Latent excitation (left) and emission (right) PSFs estimated jointly with the specimen by the proposed blind DIP approach on experimental tubulin data. Both exhibit a localized central peak, with additional diffuse and peripheral intensity. 5 Conclusion We presented a blind DIP approach for jointly estimating the specimen image and the excitation and emission PSFs for ISM imaging. By constructing each detector-dependent effective PSF from the shared excitation and emission PSFs and the detector geometry, the method incorporates the physical relationships among the kernels. On experimental tubulin data, the resulting reconstruction reveals fine filament details and estimates PSFs that differ from the theoretical model. These qualitative results support further investigation of blind DIP for ISM, including the stability and physical interpretation of the recovered PSFs and quantitative validation on suitable reference measurements.
